guide.description: ffprobe <file> prints a summary of a media file's codec, bitrate, resolution (for video), and duration — without converting anything. It works directly on a source file, or on anything ffmpeg has already written, which makes it the tool to reach for right after a convert/scale/trim to confirm the settings actually took effect.

examples.note: probing a source file directly, no conversion involved

exercises.title: Probe a video source directly
exercises.task: Use ffprobe to print raw-interview.mov's summary, with no conversion involved.
hints: ffprobe reads a file's media metadata directly — no -i, no output file

exercises.title: Probe an audio source
exercises.task: Use ffprobe to print podcast-ep1.wav's summary.
hints: Same command shape, a different file

criteria.label: Prints podcast-ep1.wav's summary — no resolution, since it's audio

exercises.title: Convert, then probe the result
exercises.task: Convert raw-interview.mov to highlight.mp4, then use ffprobe (not cat) to print its summary.
hints: First convert with ffmpeg -i raw-interview.mov highlight.mp4
Then ffprobe highlight.mp4 to see the summary

exercises.title: Put it together: trim, then probe to confirm
exercises.task: Convert raw-interview.mov to clip.mp4, keeping only the first 60 seconds with -t, then use ffprobe on clip.mp4 to confirm the new duration.
hints: -t caps the output at that many seconds from the start
ffmpeg -i raw-interview.mov -t 60 clip.mp4, then ffprobe clip.mp4
